findings.impact: A caller supplies any organisation id and receives that organisation's notes — id, owner, status, title and body for up to 5000 field inspections — bypassing both the membership check the HTTP route performs and the Firestore rules, which the Admin SDK does not evaluate.
findings.recommendation: Reject when request.auth is absent, then load the caller's profile and verify the requested orgId is in their orgs list, exactly as the /notes/recent route does.

triage.reason: orgId comes from request.data at line 89, which is the caller-supplied callable payload, and it selects the collection that is read.
No working mitigation is being stretched: the membership check that exists elsewhere in the file is simply absent here, which was verified by reading both handlers.
The missing control is the authorization decision for a bulk export, not a defence-in-depth measure.

scope.established_by: Read every handler in the file and checked each for a request.auth or profile lookup: /notes/recent has one at lines 47-50, this callable has none, and neither adminApi route has one.

findings.title: Storage update rule drops the owner, size and content-type checks
findings.class: Broken access control on object storage
findings.evidence: The update rule is 'request.auth != null' alone. The create rule directly above it (lines 14-17) requires noteOwner() == request.auth.uid, a size below 15 MB and a content type matching image/* or application/pdf; the read and delete rules (lines 12 and 22) both require ownership too. Update is the only verb in the block with none of those conditions.
findings.impact: Any authenticated user overwrites any existing attachment on any note in any organisation with content of any type and any size — replacing evidence photographs on another inspector's field note, planting an HTML or script payload at a path the app treats as an image, and defeating the upload size limit.
findings.recommendation: Give update the same predicate as create: owner check, size bound and content-type match. A rotate-or-crop re-upload is an update by the owner, which that predicate already permits.

triage.reason: The untrusted writer is any authenticated Storage client; notes.js:59-61 shows the client performing exactly this kind of upload to a client-chosen path.
The mitigations in this block were read and credited — create, read and delete are all correctly constrained. Update is the one verb that is not, so no adjacent rule compensates.
The rule itself grants the access; no misbehaving caller needs to be postulated.

scope.established_by: Compared all four verbs inside the same path match block; ownership appears in three of the four predicates, and the size and content-type constraints appear only on create.
scope.narrowed_by: The object must already exist for update to apply, so the attacker overwrites existing attachments rather than creating new ones at arbitrary paths — create still requires ownership.

findings.title: Shared note body is written to innerHTML
findings.evidence: Every other value in the function is written with textContent — the heading at line 30 and both definition-list fields at lines 9-11 — but note.body is assigned to article.innerHTML. The body is stored exactly as the client supplied it: notes.js:31-40 writes the field with no sanitisation, and neither the Firestore rules nor any function filters it on the way in or out.
findings.impact: A note body containing markup executes in the origin of the app when a supervisor opens the share view. The page holds the viewer's Firebase session, so the payload can read their profile, write to the profiles document that governs their role, and call the unauthenticated admin function from an authenticated context.
findings.recommendation: Render the body with textContent, or sanitise it through a vetted HTML sanitiser at render time if rich text is genuinely required.

triage.reason: The writer is traced: createNote at notes.js:31 and updateNote at notes.js:44 write the body field from client input, and the org-wide write rule at firestore.rules:46 lets any member of the org write another member's note.
The sink is in this function, and the surrounding lines show the author using the safe API for every other field.
There is no sanitiser anywhere on this path to credit; grep finds no escaping or sanitisation helper in the web sources.

scope.established_by: Read the whole render function to confirm this is the only non-textContent assignment, then traced note.body back through notes.js to its unsanitised writes.

findings.title: Org-wide subcollection rule overrides per-note ownership
findings.evidence: The recursive wildcard grants read and write on every document beneath an org to any member of that org. Notes actually live at orgs/<orgId>/notes (notes.js:19 builds the collection path that way, and functions/index.js:52 reads the same path), so this rule — not the ownership-scoped /notes/{noteId} block at lines 35-39 — is what governs field notes in practice. The top-level rule matches a collection the client code never writes to.
findings.impact: Any member of an organisation reads, edits and deletes every other inspector's field notes, contrary to the ownership model the ruleset states at line 34 and enforces on the unused top-level path. This is also the write primitive that makes the share-view scripting issue exploitable against colleagues.
findings.recommendation: Replace the recursive wildcard with explicit per-collection matches, and give orgs/{orgId}/notes/{noteId} the same ownership predicate the top-level notes block already has.

triage.reason: The collection path was confirmed against the client and function code (notes.js:19, functions/index.js:52), so the claim that notes live under the wildcard is read from the code rather than inferred from the rule file alone.
The untrusted actor is any org member operating the Firestore client SDK directly, which notes.js demonstrates is how the app reaches these documents.
Rules are the enforcement layer for direct client access, so this is the control rather than an extra one.

scope.established_by: Matched every Firestore path used by the client and the functions against the rule blocks: orgs/<id>/notes matches only the recursive wildcard, and the /notes/{noteId} block at line 35 matches no path the code actually uses.
scope.narrowed_by: The caller must be a member of the organisation — but membership is itself self-assignable through the profiles write rule at firestore.rules:31, so this narrowing does not hold against a determined attacker.

findings.title: Audit records are client-addressable and overwritable
findings.evidence: The document id is built from client-supplied values — orgId and seq both come from normalizeRequest(req.body) at line 60 — and the write uses .set() at line 62, which replaces any existing document rather than failing. No check confirms that the caller belongs to orgId or owns the note being sealed. The rules file describes this collection as an 'Immutable trail written by the audit function with the Admin SDK' and denies all client writes (firestore.rules:50-53), but the Admin SDK is not subject to rules.
findings.impact: Any holder of a valid Firebase ID token overwrites an existing audit record by naming its orgId and seq, replacing the sealedBy and noteId of a prior seal, or fabricates audit entries for organisations they have no relationship with. The one collection meant to be tamper-evident is neither append-only nor authorised.
findings.recommendation: Let the server generate the audit id (add() or a uuid), use create semantics so an existing id fails, and verify the caller's membership of orgId and access to the note before writing.

triage.reason: orgId and seq come from the request body at line 60; the sanitiser at lines 34-35 strips characters but preserves the caller's ability to choose the value.

The mitigations present were credited: requireIdToken does run on this app (line 43) and normalizeRequest does prevent path injection into the document reference. Neither addresses authorization or overwrite semantics.
The handler chooses .set() and derives the id from input; no caller misuse is required.

scope.established_by: Read the handler alongside the audits rule block; the write path is the only writer to that collection in the corpus, and the rules confirm it is meant to be the sole, trusted one.
scope.narrowed_by: A valid Firebase ID token is required, since requireIdToken is mounted on this app at index.js:43 — unlike adminApi, this route is at least authenticated.

findings.title: Every signed-in user can read every inspector profile
findings.evidence: The read rule is 'signedIn()' with no relationship requirement. auth.js:24-30 shows each profile carries displayName, email, role and the full orgs list. Any authenticated account — including one created through the self-service register path at auth.js:35 — can therefore enumerate the whole user directory.
findings.impact: Discloses the email address, role and organisation memberships of every inspector to any account holder, which is both a privacy exposure and useful reconnaissance for the escalation and impersonation paths reported elsewhere in this module.
findings.recommendation: Restrict profile reads to the subject and to members of a shared organisation, and move email out of the client-readable document if a directory view is required.

triage.reason: This is an access-control predicate on personal data, not a missing response header or a mock fixture.
Any authenticated client reads the collection directly through the Firestore SDK; no server handler mediates it.
Not a resource-exhaustion concern.

scope.established_by: Read the rule and cross-referenced the document shape written by auth.js:24-30 to establish which fields the permission actually exposes.
scope.narrowed_by: An authenticated account is required, though the app allows self-service registration (auth.js:35-39), so obtaining one is not a meaningful barrier.

findings.title: Cloud Function CORS reflects any requesting origin
findings.evidence: A single cors({ origin: true }) instance is created at line 15 and mounted on both express apps, at line 42 for api and at line 72 for adminApi. origin: true echoes the requesting Origin header back in access-control-allow-origin. The comment at lines 10-14 justifies this on the grounds that callers authenticate with a bearer token rather than a cookie — which is true of api, where requireIdToken is mounted, but not of adminApi, which has no authentication at all.
findings.impact: For adminApi, reflecting the origin means a page on any site can both call the unauthenticated admin routes and read their responses, turning the missing authentication into a drive-by member-list disclosure from a visitor's browser. For api the reasoning in the comment holds and the exposure is negligible.
findings.recommendation: Restrict the origin list to the portal domains, and in any case fix the missing authentication on adminApi — the CORS setting only determines whether the attacker can read the response, not whether the request executes.

triage.reason: Rule 02 excludes missing hardening headers. Here a header is present and grants read access that the same-origin policy would otherwise deny, on an endpoint with no other access control.
The bearer-token reasoning in the comment was accepted for the app where it applies; the finding is confined to the mount where the premise is false.
The Origin header is attacker-controlled, and origin: true reflects it verbatim.

scope.established_by: One cors instance is constructed in the file; grepped corsMiddleware to enumerate its two mounts, both listed above. The onCall export at line 88 uses the Firebase callable protocol and does not go through this middleware.
scope.narrowed_by: Credentials are not enabled and the api app requires a bearer token the browser never attaches automatically, so the practical exposure is confined to the unauthenticated adminApi mount at index.js:72.
